papers.title: Tight Bounds on the Randomized Communication Complexity of Vector-in-Subspace
papers.abstract: We prove that the randomized communication complexity of Vector-in-Subspace in $\mathbb R^n$ with error at most $1/3$ is $\Theta(\sqrt n)$. Alice holds a unit vector $u$ and Bob holds an $n/2$-dimensional subspace $H$; they must distinguish $u\in H$ from $u\in H^\perp$. An exact one-way quantum protocol uses $O(\log n)$ qubits, making the problem a geometric example of an exponential quantum advantage over interactive classical communication. Our lower bound matches Raz's $O(\sqrt n)$ upper bound, improves the $\Omega(n^{1/3})$ lower bound of Klartag and Regev, and removes the total-rank restriction in Grupel's $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ result. The proof establishes a Gaussian moment bound over complete rectangle partitions. A complex Gaussian representation yields a vanishing even moment whose cancellation is preserved when averaging over the partition. We control the signed conditional moments around a real center by decomposing conditional Gaussian measures into fixed coordinates and sub-Gaussian components. Combining this estimate with spherical harmonic analysis gives the communication lower bound.

papers.title: Can Quantum Layers offer Performance and Security Advantages in Vision-Language Models?
papers.abstract: As quantum computing moves from the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era toward early fault-tolerant quantum computing (EFTQC), quantum-enhanced AI is shifting from a conceptual idea to experimental research. Quantum components are expected to extend the capabilities of existing AI systems, yet it remains unclear how such components will help within large multimodal models. In this study, we try to answer that question for vision-language models (VLMs) using classically simulated quantum layers. With LLaVA-OneVision as the backbone, we evaluate 4- and 8-qubit basic-ring and strongly entangling circuits at four insertion and four replacement locations. Insertion adds quantum layers to the classical model, while replacement substitutes them for classical components. Using the same setup, we compare performance and computational cost between classical and quantum-classical hybrid models. On the Visual Spatial Reasoning dataset, inserting a quantum layer after the visual projector reaches 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 percentage-points above classical full fine-tuning. Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer retains 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters. Quantum insertion can thus improve accuracy, and selective replacement can reduce parameters. These benefits depend strongly on where the quantum layer is inserted or which classical component it replaces: earlier replacements lower accuracy, and fewer parameters do not reliably shorten training or reduce computation. To assess potential security benefits, we evaluated the robustness of quantum-classical hybrid models under six attack settings. Overall, our study maps where quantum layers help and hurt within VLMs, offering a starting point for hybrid VLM design; whether these gains generalize remains open. The code is available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/QuantumVLM.

papers.title: PQ-Vault: Provably Quantum-Safe Asset Custody for Unmodified Ethereum
papers.abstract: A quantum computer could recover the key of any Ethereum account whose public key appears on chain. We prove that no sidechain or bridge that leaves Ethereum's rules unchanged can protect such accounts: their funds must move into a contract whose release condition relies only on quantum-safe primitives. We design \emph{PQ-Vault}, a custody system for unmodified Ethereum combining this vault, a quantum-safe proof-of-stake sidechain whose checkpoints carry compact certificates, and an optimistic dispute protocol. We give the first security proof of compact certificates against quantum attackers and a matching attack: with classically chosen parameters, the guarantee falls from 128 to about 60 bits, and a simple rule restores it. We show that a common seed-update rule in hash-chain proof of stake lets an attacker steer chosen slots and profit from splitting its stake, and give an election whose steering gain and inclusion delay are provably bounded against quantum attackers. Since compressing certificates with a pairing-based SNARK breaks quantum security, we use fraud proofs that need a single signature check. For 65,536 validators, a certificate is 0.8 MB, 260 times smaller than all signatures, and verifies in about 20 ms; the vault accepts a checkpoint for about 420,000 gas.

papers.title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization Process for Data Imputation
papers.abstract: Data imputation is a critical preprocessing step, particularly in clinical datasets where missingness can bias downstream inference. We propose a quantum-inspired imputation framework and evaluate it on the UCI Pima Indians Diabetes dataset, where several physiological variables contain structural zeros that are treated as missing. The approach combines Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with quantum rotation-based reconstruction, where rotation angles are selected via gradient-free optimizers (Simulated Annealing, COBYLA, and Differential Evolution). For robustness, we retain the top three optimizer solutions per method and reconstruct missing values under distribution-aware bounds (e.g., $\pm 2$ standard deviations) and avoid unrealistic collapse toward central tendency. We also benchmark against (i) classical baselines (Mean, KNN, MICE, Decision Tree), (ii) modern matrix/ML imputers (SoftImpute, MissForest, VAE), and (iii) rotation/PCA controls (random orthogonal rotations and bootstrap PCA). Across the evaluated features, quantum-inspired variants achieve substantially improved distributional fidelity under Wasserstein W1 relative to modern baselines (e.g., the best quantum setting reduces average W1 by $\sim$66% vs. SoftImpute, $\sim$84% vs. MissForest, and $\sim$90% vs. VAE; and by $\sim$60% vs. Mean imputation), while remaining competitive with strong classical/control configurations. Dispersion is better preserved under the quantum-inspired methods, with variance/SD ratios closer to the observed data than (SoftImpute, MissForest, and VAE) and typically better than (Mean, KNN, MICE, and Decision Tree) on average. Overall, the results support quantum-inspired, optimization-guided rotations as a statistically grounded and scalable strategy for realistic imputation in healthcare and general AI pipelines, with a design that can be mapped to future quantum hardware as it matures.

papers.title: A parity obstruction to degree-optimal syndrome extraction in bivariate bicycle codes
papers.abstract: Syndrome extraction for a CSS code has depth at least the Tanner-graph degree $\Delta$, attained by edge colouring if gate order is ignored; correctness adds a parity constraint. We prove three general obstructions to depth-$\Delta$ extraction and show that, for every two-block group-algebra code with weight-three polynomials whose checks overlap in at most two qubits, no correct single-round circuit with one ancilla per check and one CNOT per Tanner edge has depth six: the minimum is seven, so the seven-layer cycle of Bravyi \emph{et al.} is optimal for their seven bivariate bicycle codes. This is the first analytic, family-wide impossibility result, extending prior instance-specific solver-based infeasibility results. The hypothesis cannot be dropped: a single orbit of four-qubit overlaps with a collision element of even order and $2$-height at most eight makes depth six attainable, and a $[[72,8,6]]$ code of this kind has a verified six-layer circuit. The refutations carry DRAT certificates.

papers.title: Evolutionary BP+OSD Decoding for Low-Latency Quantum Error Correction
papers.abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) for fault-tolerant quantum computing requires a balanced decoding solution that offers high performance, low complexity, and low latency. However, the de facto standard - belief propagation (BP) combined with ordered statistics decoding (OSD) - suffers from excessive iterations in the BP stage and high complexity in the OSD stage. To address these challenges, we propose an evolutionary BP (EBP) decoder optimized via a differential evolution (DE) algorithm. By leveraging the gradient-free nature of DE, we enable end-to-end optimization of the EBP+OSD structure to maximize overall performance. In addition, a multi-objective selection rule is introduced to suppress frequent OSD activation, significantly reducing complexity overhead. Simulation results on surface codes and quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes demonstrate that EBP+OSD simultaneously achieves both superior decoding performance and substantially lower complexity compared to conventional BP+OSD, particularly in stringent low-latency regimes.

papers.title: Graph-Theoretic Formulation of Hamiltonian and Ground-State Sign Structures in Heisenberg Antiferromagnets
papers.abstract: We study Heisenberg antiferromagnets through a graph-theoretic representation of their Hamiltonians. In the computational basis of a fixed-magnetization sector, the Heisenberg Hamiltonian equals a constant minus the weighted Laplacian of a graph whose vertices are spin configurations and whose edges connect configurations related by exchanging two antiparallel spins on a lattice bond. We call this graph the Hilbert graph (HG) which is isomorphic to the token graph of the lattice over which the Hamiltonian is defined. The exact ground-state energy is then determined by the largest eigenvalue of the HG Laplacian, which is the spectral relaxation of weighted Max-Cut on the HG. With the amplitudes fixed, the phase-dependent part of the variational energy defines an antiferromagnetic classical XY model on the HG, with couplings set by the amplitudes. Restricting the variational state to be real, i.e., restricting its phases to $\{0,\pi\}$, reduces the fixed-amplitude energy minimization to solving an antiferromagnetic Ising model and hence a weighted Max-Cut on the HG. When the weights are generated from non-degenerate ground-state amplitudes, the optimal phases give the ground-state sign structure which can be recovered from the weights in time polynomial in the size of the HG. On the Hamiltonian side, a diagonal sign transformation removes all positive off-diagonal matrix elements if and only if the HG is bipartite, which reproduces the Marshall sign rule on bipartite lattices through the graph two-coloring problem; otherwise, the minimal remaining positive weight equals the sum of HG edge weights left uncut by the Max-Cut. This graph formulation establishes a common framework for understanding wave function sign structure, Hamiltonian stoquasticity, non-convexity of phase optimization in variational Monte Carlo, and the average sign in quantum Monte Carlo.

papers.title: Long-horizon autoformalization of a core theorem underlying MIP* = RE
papers.abstract: Landmark mathematical formalizations have taken specialist teams years to complete. We present FormalFlow, a system that coordinates AI proving agents under human supervision to address statement drift and proof composition in long-horizon formalization. Drawing on software-engineering principles and practices, it uses a shared blueprint to guide nested planning, proving, and review loops. Using FormalFlow, we completed a machine-checked Lean 4 proof of the quantum soundness of the classical low individual-degree test, a core theorem underlying MIP* = RE, in 63 days. The final library contains 126,367 lines of Lean code, all generated by agents. Beyond providing a verified foundation for quantum complexity, the formalization corrects side conditions and intermediate error bounds in the published proof and improves the error exponent of the main theorem. The development record shows what it takes to trust proofs written by AI agents and provides reusable tools for verifying research mathematics at scale.

papers.title: Hidden parabolic subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ over finite chain rings
papers.abstract: We give a bounded-error quantum polynomial-time algorithm for finding hidden parabolic subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ over any effectively presented finite chain ring $R$. We call auxiliary group elements or subgroups used to extract information through oracle queries \emph{probes}. For chain length at least two, elementary abelian socle probes first recover the complete flag modulo the maximal ideal. When the residue field has size $q\ge3$, we reconstruct the flag recursively, lifting rank-one terminal members one digit at a time. The intermediate digits reduce to abelian hidden subgroup problems, while the final digit is a finite-field multiple-shift problem solved using learning from subset and Fourier sampling. For $q=2$, where distinct flags can have the same stabilizer, we instead lift the conjugate parabolic subgroup through the congruence filtration. A final linear system determines it modulo normalizer directions. The algorithm outputs generators with probability at least $1-\epsilon$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\log|R|,\log(1/\epsilon))$. Consequences include $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})$ for every $N\ge2$ and, with an explicit maximal-order presentation, $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathcal{O}_K/N\mathcal{O}_K)$ for number fields $K$.

papers.title: Engineering Low-Latency, High-Throughput Quantum Decoders on NVIDIA GPUs
papers.abstract: We design and optimize a quantum error correction (QEC) decoder for NVIDIA GPUs, combining Relay belief propagation, a state-of-the-art message-passing algorithm, with order-zero ordered statistics post-processing. Our implementation uses CUDA Graphs to control GPU execution, stops updates for converged samples, and collects unresolved samples in queues for post-processing. We optimize sparse traversal through coalesced message accesses, prefetching, and register reuse, and accelerate binary post-processing with warp-level collectives. In addition, mixed FP16-FP32 arithmetic and INT8 quantization reduce message storage and traffic while retaining accuracy using accumulators at higher precision. We evaluate surface, hypergraph product, and bivariate bicycle code workloads on NVIDIA A100 and GH200 data-center GPUs and a commodity RTX 5080. On the bivariate bicycle code at error probability 0.003, INT8 halves amortized decoding time relative to independently tuned FP32 with a negligible logical error rate increase on RTX 5080. With independent syndrome batches submitted back-to-back to concurrent decoder instances, RTX 5080 delivers 91% of GH200's highest measured throughput with an 8.9x shorter median submission-to-correction latency. The combination of performance optimization, mixed precision, INT8 quantization, and concurrent decoder instances opens a path toward QEC decoder clusters built from commodity GPUs.

papers.title: Pauli Decomposition by Character Theory: A Memory-Bounded Algorithm for Qubits and Qudits
papers.abstract: Pauli decomposition of an $n$-qubit operator is expensive if each of the $4^n$ Pauli strings is treated as an unstructured object. Labeling those strings by the configuration space $(\mathbb{Z}_2)^n$ makes them displacement operators $X^{\otimes x}Z^{\otimes z}$ on the computational space: shifts by~$x$ and multiplications by characters $Z^{\otimes z}$ in the computational basis. That labeling organizes the operator into $2^n$ fibers of length $2^n$, one per shift~$x$, each collecting the computational-basis amplitudes that hop by~$x$. Expanding each fiber function in the character basis of $(\mathbb{Z}_2)^n$ --- a length-$2^n$ Walsh--Hadamard transform --- recovers the Pauli coefficients at total cost $O(n\cdot4^n)$. The same fiber / shift--character picture extends to $(\mathbb{Z}_p)^n$ (Heisenberg--Weyl qudits). \texttt{paulikit} is a memory-bounded realization for qubits: for matrix-sparse inputs, peak memory need not densify to a full $2^n\times2^n$ operator. Performance is checked on a stated low-end GNU/Linux platform for a coupled-oscillator sweep beyond a billion Pauli terms.

papers.title: Quantum f-divergences from retrodiction: a unifying classical variational principle
papers.abstract: The same classical f-divergence admits inequivalent extensions to quantum states. The question is whether these extensions can be obtained from a common operational variational principle. Here we generalize Matsumoto's reverse-test optimization by introducing a reference prior state. More explicitly, we minimize the statistical distinguishability between a forward and a reverse prepare-and-measure process, related by retrodiction through the chosen reference and subject to prescribed quantum averages. Distinguishability is quantified by the classical f-divergence between their complete records. For faithful states in finite dimension, we prove that the same spectral implementation attains the minimum simultaneously for every operator-convex f. Varying the reference allows us to interpolate between standard and maximal quantum f-divergences of the prescribed states, passing through the geodesic family. More precisely, a flat reference yields the standard quantum f-divergences, thereby giving the Nussbaum-Szko{\l}a distributions a variational characterization as optimal records. Choosing either prescribed state as reference recovers maximal quantum f-divergences and Matsumoto's reverse tests, while power references realize the geodesic interpolation. In the relative-entropy case, this gives the passage from Umegaki to Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy by changing the prior for retrodiction.

papers.title: Benchmarking the Quantum Leap: Auditing LLM Evaluation for Quantum Code Generation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate quantum programs, but reliable evaluation remains difficult because benchmarks differ in task composition, scoring, and failure handling. We evaluate 15 hosted frontier, open-weight, quantum-specialized, and retrieval-augmented models on five quantum code-generation suites (530 tasks), plus 10 models on our new QuantumBenchEval (QBE) benchmark (96 tasks across six topics). We report bootstrap confidence intervals, multiplicity-adjusted paired comparisons, and audits of output validity and evaluator behavior. QiskitHumanEval-Standard approaches saturation (98.7% pass@1), while its Hard variant retains headroom (63.8%). None of the five top-two comparisons across primary suites remains significant after multiple-comparison correction. Evaluator design substantially changes scores: removing checks for unspecified quantities raises GPT-6 Astra's QBE pass@1 from 0% to 94.1% (T1) and from 1.2% to 92.9% (T6), without changing model outputs. We identify 17 QuanBench-117 tasks with shared failures linked to benchmark-owned imports. Controlled probes also reveal unexecuted unit tests, leakage of canonical functions into candidate execution, and reference imports that block otherwise valid candidates. These defects can produce both false failures and false passes, so historical QuanBench results require revalidation under an isolated evaluator. Overall, leaderboard scores alone do not adequately characterize progress in quantum code generation. We release our harness, per-sample results, and audit artifacts and recommend validating evaluators, isolating candidate code, and reporting uncertainty and output validity.

papers.title: Turning Quantum Compiler Configuration Selection Upside Down: A Top-Down Paradigm
papers.abstract: Selecting an effective quantum compiler configuration requires coordinated decisions over both hardware targets and compiler settings, with the ultimate goal of improving circuit execution fidelity. Existing SOTA approaches typically decompose this problem into two sequential stages: a device is chosen first, after which compiler options are tuned on that device through RL-based search. This bottom-up strategy can be fundamentally limited by its initial device decision, since a poorly matched backend may constrain the best fidelity achievable regardless of how effectively later compiler options are optimized. In contrast to classical compiler tuning, where the search space is often prohibitively large, the configuration space of quantum compilers remains manageable enough to support exhaustive search. Consequently, rather than repeatedly searching from candidate configurations, one can derive reusable configuration knowledge from offline oracle results and apply it directly to new circuits. In this paper, we introduce a top-down configuration-selection paradigm and build QuOPTBench, an exhaustively searched benchmark containing oracle configurations for 268 quantum circuits. We first study whether LLMs can directly infer suitable configurations and evaluate ten representative LLMs. The results reveal that vanilla LLMs remain far from the oracle. We then employ an LLM to extract transferable rules from sampled circuits governing configuration selection. Using these rules together with predictors trained on the enumerated configuration data of the sampled circuits, we design QuTOP, a rule-guided ML framework that performs fast configuration selection without iterative online search. Across our evaluation, the distilled rules consistently strengthen LLM-based selection, while QuTOP provides the strongest overall balance between solution quality and selection latency among the baselines.

papers.title: Classification of bipartite observables II: NIP observables and the Todorcevic trichotomy
papers.abstract: This is the second of a series of three papers that bring model theory to quantum information. The dividing lines of Shelah's classification theory, which separate the tame first-order theories from the wild ones, become properties of bipartite observables: properties of the expectation values obtained when two independently prepared quantum systems are idealized one after the other. In this paper we focus on Shelah's independence property. An observable without it has idealized responses of the first Baire class, and Todor\v{c}evi\'c's trichotomy for Rosenthal compacta divides such observables into three classes, each containing a physical order. In the transverse-field Ising model, the spontaneous magnetization decides whether the family of magnetizations is stable or lies in the second class.

papers.title: Methods for Deriving Nonlinear Kinetic Equations from the Dynamics of Quantum Systems
papers.abstract: The article outlines key topics related to deriving kinetic equations and, in general, to the relationship between the evolution equations governing quantum many-particle systems. The main issues being considered are the mathematical origin of quantum kinetic equations, novel methods for deriving kinetic equations from hierarchies of evolution equations for quantum systems, specifically focusing on kinetics within the framework of the evolution of observables, and the generalization of the quantum kinetic equation specified by non-separable initial states.

papers.title: Lieb-Robinson bounds via the Combes-Thomas estimate
papers.abstract: This paper studies quantum spin systems: networks of spins coupled by local interactions. The Lieb-Robinson bound predicts that in these systems, information propagates at an essentially finite speed. We produce a new proof of this result. Our approach relies on a spectral bound on entries of resolvents of band matrices, the Combes-Thomas estimate, rather than on the standard path-counting argument.

papers.title: The L\'{e}vy wave packet and fractional uncertainty relations
papers.abstract: This work revisits the debate on fractional uncertainty relations that arose a decade ago and tries to settle it. After a careful study of the position-momentum uncertainty product of the L\'{e}vy wave packet, a novel lower bound is proposed for uncertainty relations in fractional quantum mechanics. This bound is nearly linear in the L\'{e}vy index and is satisfied by exact, calculable solutions available in the literature.

papers.title: Quantum Charge as a Particle/Antiparticle Label
papers.abstract: We show that the concept of particles and antiparticles is related to the Weyl-Heisenberg group $W\!H_3$. Its generators are the position operators $\hat x^a$, the momentum operators $\hat p_a$, and the central element $Q_{\sf{v}}$, which defines a subgroup U(1)$_{\sf v}$ of $W\!H_3$. We show that the wave functions have a charge relative to the group U(1)$_{\sf{v}}$ equal to either $q_+=1/\hbar$ (particle $\psi_+$) or $q_-=-1/\hbar$ (antiparticle $\psi_-$). We call these eigenvalues of the operator $Q_{\sf{v}}$ quantum charges: $Q_{\sf{v}}\psi_\pm^{}=q_\pm^{}\psi_\pm^{}$. The wave functions $\psi_+$ and $\psi_-$ belong to the Hilbert spaces $\mathcal{H}_+$ and $\mathcal{H}_-$, on which unitarily inequivalent representations $\pi_\hbar$ and $\pi_{-\hbar}$ of the Weyl-Heisenberg group $W\!H_3$ are defined. These representations are related to each other by the antilinear charge conjugation operator $\hat C$, which maps $\mathcal{H}_+, q_+$ to $\mathcal{H}_-, q_-$. Charges $q_\pm^{}$ are intrinsic characteristics of the wave functions $\psi_\pm^{}$, similar to spin and electric charge. The wave function possesses one of these charges, $q_+$ or $q_-$, prior to the specification of any equations. We show that negative probabilities/energies and the Klein paradox in Klein-Gordon and Dirac theories are consequences of the violation of U(1)$_{\sf v}$-invariance in these theories. Restoring this invariance separates particle and antiparticles and eliminates all paradoxes at the level of first-quantized relativistic theories.

papers.title: The Prevalence of Straight Shots in Control Space for Reaching Optimal Quantum Performance
papers.abstract: Gradient-based algorithms are often applied to identify an optimal control for maximizing a quantum objective functional by following a steepest ascent path to the top of the control landscape. In contrast, this paper explores straight shots through control space where movement along such a path corresponds to a less demanding monotonic complete climb up the landscape for the optimal objective value. Existing studies of control landscapes have revealed the presence of straight shots, but identifying them required computationally intensive stochastic methods. In this paper, we introduce a non-stochastic straight-shot search algorithm (STSA) that identifies a large class of straight shots. We apply STSA to numerically generate more than 10,000 distinct straight-shot optimization paths and analyze their statistical distribution for each of the objectives of (i) state-to-state transitions, (ii) general observables, and (iii) unitary transformation generation. The results show a decrease in the nearest-neighbor distances among straight shots as the sample size increases, suggesting their prevalence in control space. We further conjecture that the starting locations of the straight-shot pathways on a landscape level set may form connected neighborhoods, motivating future investigation into their underlying topological structure. The present paper focuses on the use of STSA for locating massive numbers of straight solutions. However, the STSA is not a high-efficiency algorithm in its present form, but the discovered prevalence of control straight shots leaves open future advances to accelerate the discovery of straight shots as optimal controls.

papers.title: Adapted Fr\"ohlich-Pizzo Model for Horizon-Induced Decoherence
papers.abstract: The Fr\"ohlich-Pizzo (FP) model is a quantum-mechanical model originally developed to describe the interaction between an atom and the electromagnetic field in the nonrelativistic limit $c\to\infty$. We show that an adaptation of the FP model based on the local algebras of a $U(1)$ chiral current captures essential features of the horizon-induced decoherence mechanism identified by Danielson, Satishchandran, and Wald (DSW) in the limit of large holding time $T$. Our analysis suggests that the effective dynamics of the system undergoing decoherence in the DSW setting retains non-Markovian features. Our approach also offers a glimpse into the possible role of quantum events in the dynamics underlying horizon-induced decoherence.

papers.title: Finite Classification of Transversal Diagonal Gates Beyond Stabilizer Codes
papers.abstract: We establish that transversal diagonal gates on exact qubit codes of distance at least two can be exhaustively classified within a finite search space. Although code-preserving physical gates can have continuous phases, any projective logical action induced by a transversal diagonal gate can always be realized by a physical gate of finite order. Crucially, we prove that this physical order has an upper bound determined solely by the code parameters. This order bound enables the subset-sum-linear-programming (SSLP) framework introduced in arXiv:2504.20847 to exhaustively enumerate all candidate discrete symmetries, after which the Knill-Laflamme equations determine the remaining continuous code parameters. Applying this method to the nontrivial diagonal sector of exact $((6,2,3))$ codes, SSLP yields $66$ candidate symmetry classes, of which exactly $15$ are realizable, supporting full projective diagonal logical cyclic groups of orders $2$, $3$, and $5$. In particular, for order $5$, the code is unique up to local unitaries and qubit permutations, equivalent to the code constructed in arXiv:2504.20847. This code also attains the minimum length $n=6$ among exact $((n, 2, \ge 3))$ codes whose full projective transversal group cannot be conjugated into the projective Clifford group.

papers.title: Edge universality in Floquet sideband spectra
papers.abstract: A monochromatic voltage drive redistributes noninteracting fermions over sidebands with Bessel amplitudes. A sharp Fermi step gives the discrete Bessel source kernel, whose large amplitude edge has the Airy limit known from random matrices and propagating fronts. At zero temperature and for energy independent transmission, the deficit of the dc bias derivative of low frequency partition noise from its large bias slope is proportional to the kernel diagonal, with ac amplitude fixed. Shifting the integer threshold coordinate down by half a sideband removes the leading finite amplitude correction. For reservoirs at a common temperature, we derive the rescaled deficit's crossover through one thermal convolution per reservoir. Its leading low temperature correction is twice that of the rescaled source occupation. We specify the geometry and mode resolution needed to distinguish this signature from the full Airy point process.

papers.title: Depth dependence of entanglement and circuit complexity in random linear optical networks
papers.abstract: We study the growth of entanglement and circuit complexity in random passive linear optical networks as a function of the circuit depth. For entanglement dynamics, we start with an initial Gaussian state with all $n$ modes equally squeezed. For random brickwork circuits, we show that entanglement, as measured by the R\'enyi-2 entropy, grows diffusively as a function of the depth, in contrast to the linear growth for random qubit brickwork circuits. In the other direction, for arbitrary circuit geometries we prove bounds on depths which ensure the average-case subsystem entanglement reaches within a constant factor of the maximum value in all subsystems, and bounds which ensure closeness of the random linear optical unitary to a Haar random unitary in $L^2$ Wasserstein distance. We also consider robust circuit complexity for random one-dimensional brickwall circuits, as measured by the minimum number of gates required in any circuit that approximately implements the linear optical unitary. Viewing this as a function of the number of modes and the circuit depth, we show the robust circuit complexity for random one-dimensional brickwall circuits scales at most diffusively in the depth with high probability, again in contrast to the linear scaling for certain random qubit circuits. The corresponding Gaussian unitary $\tilde{\mathcal U}$ for the approximate implementation retains high output fidelity $|\langle\psi|\mathcal U^\dagger \tilde{\mathcal U}|\psi\rangle|^2$ for pure states $|\psi\rangle$ with constrained expected photon-number.

papers.title: Exact quantum circuits for a lattice Boltzmann realization of the Dirac equation
papers.abstract: The quantum lattice Boltzmann scheme of Succi and Dellar advances a four-component Dirac spinor on a lattice by a fixed sequence of local, exactly norm-preserving operations: a basis rotation, a collision, a streaming shift, and the inverse rotation. While this correspondence has been noted qualitatively, it has remained unclear whether it can be realized exactly and unitarily as a gate-model quantum circuit. This unitarity is a structural property of the scheme, which should, in principle, enable an operator-by-operator port onto quantum hardware. We give a gate-level construction of every operation of the three-dimensional Dirac QLB scheme: the fixed rotation gates, the collision gate, the streaming shift as a controlled increment on a position register, the position-dependent potential as a phase oracle, and periodic and reflecting boundary conditions as unitary circuits. Together, these constructions provide the first complete demonstration that the scheme is exactly representable in the gate model without any approximation beyond the classical method itself. We then compose them into single-axis, two- and three-dimensional time steps. On a state-vector emulator the resulting circuits reproduce the classical QLB solver to machine precision, thus verifying our quantum implementation. Our aim is representability and correctness rather than computational speedup; questions of state preparation, asymptotic cost, and hardware noise are identified as open avenues for future work. Appendices restore physical units, derive the scheme's Zitterbewegung in closed form and compare it with a trapped-ion simulation, and execute a reduced two-site instance on a Rigetti superconducting processor, where choosing the qubits from the live calibration lowers the state-preparation error. All operators, circuits, and figures are reproducible from the open-source quantumKineticMethods library.

papers.title: Spectral Analysis Beyond the Spectral Gap: Rapid Mixing of Quantum Gibbs Samplers in One Dimension
papers.abstract: We prove rapid mixing of a quantum Gibbs sampler for general one-dimensional non-commuting local spin systems at every fixed positive temperature. In particular, for a system of $n$ sites, we show that the Kubo--Martin--Schwinger (KMS) detailed-balanced Gibbs sampler of~\cite{CKG2023} converges from any initial state to trace-norm error $\epsilon$ in time $O(\log^4(n)+\log(1/\epsilon))$. This improves the previous $O(n+\log(1/\epsilon))$ bound and establishes rapid mixing beyond high-temperature and weak-interaction regimes. Our proof explains why the slowest decay rate, captured by the spectral gap, can substantially underestimate the speed of equilibration. The key insight is that a state far from equilibrium must have a substantial component outside the span of low-weight Pauli operators, where stronger dissipation estimates apply. This yields two stages of relaxation: a double-exponential convergence from a bad initial state, followed by exponential convergence near equilibrium. We turn this mechanism into a framework for proving rapid mixing through spectral analysis beyond the gap. Our decay estimate is equivalent to exponential convergence in sandwiched R\'enyi-2 divergence. Together with the spectral gap, it also implies a modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality with rate $\Omega(\log^{-4}(n))$.

papers.title: Finite-time quantum equilibration from local correlations
papers.abstract: An isolated quantum system evolves reversibly, yet a small subsystem can lose nearly all information about its initial state. Conserved quantities may retain some of this information, depending on how strongly they overlap with local observables. Here we consider a subsystem in an arbitrary initial state coupled to a maximally mixed bath. We show that the worst-input mean-square equilibration error, maximised over window origins, is bounded from above and below by the mean square of a complete local autocorrelation, with the stationary part subtracted. The two mean-square quantities are linearly comparable. A correlation record over a finite interval therefore controls the equilibration error in every interval of the same length, and the result extends to nonnegative observation weights with nonnegative Fourier transform. The result allows arbitrary degeneracies of energies and gaps. We apply it to two static Hamiltonian families. For fixed spin subsystems in the one-particle sector of a bounded-range periodic clock, fixed-accuracy thermalisation is guaranteed on windows that grow only slightly faster than linearly with system size, despite exponentially small positive energies. A random commuting model with logarithmic interaction range retains an extensive set of conserved observables. Its expected mean-square error is bounded by a finite-size term and an inverse-time term. The inverse-time dependence is unavoidable because of the initial transient. These examples show how local relaxation can coexist with exact conservation laws and a finely spaced spectrum.

papers.title: Correlation of divergency: c_delta. Being different in a similar way or not
papers.abstract: Matched sets may have unlike mean scores and spreads yet share the same way in which some scores stand apart. Mean gaps and raw-score correlations do not answer this question. Correlation of divergency, c_delta, is put forward to fill that gap. For every score in each of two equally sized, matched sets, it finds how far that score lies from every other score in its own set. It then draws these gaps into one divergence score through a power mean. The Pearson correlation between the two lists of divergence scores is c_delta, which lies between -1 and 1. A high positive value means that the same people or things stand out in both sets, no matter which way their raw scores point. A negative value means that a score far from the rest in one set tends to be matched with a score near the rest in the other, whilst a value near zero shows little linear link. As c_delta stems from within-set gaps, it is unchanged by shifts in overall level or units. It can show whether the same people feel sharply shut out in matched neighbourhood sets, whether the same bacterial strains grow oddly under two drugs, or whether the same proteins stand out in two drug-binding fingerprints. It should sit alongside means and raw-score correlations rather than take their place: c_delta does not show whether an outlier is high or low, nor why it arose. The power p sets the weight given to wide gaps. With p=1 it uses Gini distance, and with p=2 root-mean-square distance. Higher p gives more weight to the furthest gaps but cuts Kish's effective sample size. The raw scores and the choice of p must therefore be read with care.

papers.title: Geometry-controlled zeros of resonant Kelvin-wave conversion in four spatial dimensions
papers.abstract: Kelvin waves carry energy along vortices, but their resonant interactions contain information that is absent from the linear spectrum. We identify a geometry that exposes this information on a vortex surface in four spatial dimensions. Perpendicular incoming waves cancel the complete local-area four-wave coupling, leaving the finite nonlocal interaction mediated by the surrounding fluid. This interaction restores conversion at generic wave-number ratios, yet changes sign and vanishes at a selected ratio while momentum and frequency remain exactly matched. Matching to Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) theory, including the microscopic core response, establishes a zero of the full coupling at every sufficiently small nonzero wave number, with ratio tending to $\lambda_*\simeq1.469$. Finite-grid GP coefficients exhibit a sign reversal for the same resonant quartets. Separate coherent-mixing calculations and weak-probe spectra connect the coupling sign to the generated-wave phase and the ordering of reflection-even and reflection-odd modes. The resulting suppression removes a leading channel for changing propagation directions without changing the paired wavelengths. These results isolate a nonlinear effect of the surrounding flow that local tension misses, providing a microscopic benchmark for vortex-wave theories and a starting point for studying angular redistribution beyond the Kelvin spectrum.

papers.title: From Traveling Waves to Synthetic Gauge Fields: A Field-Free Route to Superconducting Diode Effect
papers.abstract: The superconducting diode effect requires the forward and reverse bias currents to differ, a scenario achieved via inversion and time-reversal symmetries broken together. The latter, and the more crucial one, is inevitably achieved by a magnetic field. Here, we show that a spatio-temporally driven chemical potential of the form, $\mu_j(t)=\mu+V\cos(\omega t+\kd j)$, achieves both at once. Applied to a helical Shiba chain, the drive transmutes a traveling Peierls phase via generating an odd-in-momentum term, equivalent to an imaginary next-nearest-neighbour Haldane-like hopping in real space. Remarkably, the protocol is spin-blind, which renders the time-reversal breaking via a synthetic gauge flux rather than an effective Zeeman field. The rectification is odd in the drive wavevector, with exact zeros at $\kd=n\pi$ and an analytical optimum at $\kd=2\pi/3$. It is however, even in the exchange coupling, $J$ and persists even at $J=0$. Furthermore, the rectification scales inversely with the pair-breaking gap, yielding approximately $50\%$ rectification in the topological phase and $10\%$ in the trivial phase. Symmetry breaking is thus drive-controlled, allowing it to be switched on, tuned, and reversed without an external magnetic field.
